title: Relative length of DVR lattices equals determinant valuation
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], let $K$ be its fraction field, and let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $K$-vector space [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Let $M\subseteq V$ be an $R$-submodule which is finitely generated [def-weil-finitely-generated-module] and whose $K$-linear span is $V$. Let $g:V\to V$ be a $K$-linear isomorphism and put $H=M\cap g(M)$. Write $\ell_R$ for module length [def-weil-pbc-module-length], $\det_K(g)$ for the endomorphism determinant [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant], and $v_R:K^\times\to\mathbf Z$ for the normalized valuation, defined by $v_R(ut^r)=r$ for a unit $u\in R^\times$, a uniformizer $t$ and $r\in\mathbf Z$. Then both $M/H$ and $g(M)/H$ have finite $R$-length, and, regarding those lengths as integers, $$\ell_R(M/H)-\ell_R(g(M)/H)=v_R(\det_K(g)).$$

source.place: Tag 02MI (lemma-order-vanishing-determinant), specialized to a DVR, with the finite-length assertion from Tag 02MF (lemma-compare-lattices) and the distance definition Tag 02MG (definition-distance). Order as defined in Tag 02MD (definition-ord) is the normalized uniformizer exponent for a DVR.

proof.text: The $R$-module $M$ is torsion-free: if $0\ne a\in R$ and $ax=0$ in $M\subseteq V$, multiplication by $a^{-1}\in K$ gives $x=0$. Apply [lem-sc-dvr-fg-torsionfree-free], using the assumed finite generation, to choose a finite $R$-basis $b_1,\ldots,b_n$ of $M$. This is a $K$-basis of $V$: it spans because $K M=V$, and a $K$-linear relation can be multiplied by a common nonzero denominator to give an $R$-linear relation. Consequently $g(b_1),\ldots,g(b_n)$ is both an $R$-basis of $g(M)$ and a $K$-basis of $V$. If $n=0$, then $V=M=g(M)=H=0$, the two lengths are zero by [def-weil-pbc-module-length], and the empty determinant is $1$ by [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant], so the result is $0=v_R(1)$. Henceforth assume $n>0$.

source.place: Tag 02ME (definition-lattice), remark after the definition; freeness from More on Algebra Tag 0AUW (lemma-dedekind-torsion-free-flat), part (3). The rank-zero case uses Tag 02LY (definition-length).

proof.text: Fix a uniformizer $t$. By [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], $R$ is a local principal ideal domain with nonzero maximal ideal $tR$, so $t\ne0$ and $t$ is not a unit. The Noetherianity conclusion of [lem-weil-pbc-pid-noetherian-normal] allows [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power] to be applied to $R$ and $t$. Write a nonzero fraction $a/b$ as $(u_a/u_b)t^{i-j}$ using the resulting forms $a=u_at^i$, $b=u_bt^j$. The exponent is unique: two different exponents would, after cancellation in $K$, make a positive power of the nonunit $t$ a unit in $R$. Thus the normalized exponent convention of the statement defines $v_R$ on all $K^\times$. Multiplying these expressions shows $v_R(xy)=v_R(x)+v_R(y)$, $v_R(x^{-1})=-v_R(x)$, and $v_R(u)=0$ for $u\in R^\times$. Also $t^q x\in R$ whenever $q\ge0$ and $q+v_R(x)\ge0$.

source.place: Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), final assertion and valuation calculation in the proof; Tag 02MD (definition-ord), fraction convention.

proof.text: For every integer $s\ge0$, one has $\ell_R(R/t^sR)=s$. Indeed each ideal containing $t^sR$ is nonzero and principal by [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. A generator has the form $ut^j$ by [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power], so the ideal is $t^jR$. Containment $t^sR\subseteq t^jR$ holds precisely for $j\le s$: if $j>s$, cancellation would give $1\in tR$. The ideals above $t^sR$ are therefore exactly $R,tR,\ldots,t^sR$, all distinct. The inverse image under $R\to R/t^sR$ identifies submodules of this quotient with these ideals and preserves strict inclusions, so the length definition [def-weil-pbc-module-length] gives $s$, including $s=0$. Since a unit does not change its principal ideal, $\ell_R(R/aR)=s$ whenever $a=ut^s\ne0$. More generally any $R$-linear isomorphism preserves length: image and inverse image give inverse bijections on submodule chains.

proof.text: Express each $b_j$ in the $K$-basis $(g(b_i))$: $b_j=\sum_i c_{ij}g(b_i)$ with $c_{ij}\in K$. Choose an integer $q\ge0$ at least $-v_R(c_{ij})$ for every nonzero coefficient in this finite array. Step 2 gives $t^qc_{ij}\in R$ for every coefficient, including zero. Hence every $t^qb_j$ belongs to $g(M)$. Set $N=t^qM$; then $N\subseteq M\cap g(M)=H$. It has $R$-basis $(t^qb_j)$ and $K$-span $V$, since $t^q\ne0$. We will compute $M/N$ and $g(M)/N$ using this common finite free submodule, before making any assertion that $H$ is finitely generated.

source.place: Tag 02MF (lemma-compare-lattices), proof of parts (1) and (3): clearing finitely many denominators to obtain a common sublattice, here using powers of a uniformizer.

proof.text: For either $E=M$ or $E=g(M)$, apply [lem-sc-dvr-saturation-line-smith-normal-form] to the finite free module $E$ and its submodule $N$. Obtain bases $e'_1,\ldots,e'_n$ of $E$ and $f'_1,\ldots,f'_r$ of $N$, with $r\le n$ and $f'_i=a_i e'_i$ after indexing the distinct selected coordinates first. Each $a_i\ne0$ because $f'_i\ne0$. Both bases are $K$-linearly independent by clearing denominators as in Step 1. Since $N$ spans $V$, the selected $e'_i$ span $V$; no unselected basis vector can remain, and $r=n$. By Step 2 write $a_i=u_it^{s_i}$ with $u_i\in R^\times$ and $s_i\ge0$.

source.place: DVR specialization of Tag 02MI (lemma-order-vanishing-determinant), using the existing Smith normal form leaf; its Mathlib source is LinearAlgebra/FreeModule/PID.lean, Submodule.exists_smith_normal_form_of_le:492.

proof.text: In the coordinates of the basis $(e'_i)$, send $\sum_i x_i e'_i$ to $(x_i\bmod a_iR)_i$. This surjective $R$-linear map has kernel precisely $N=\bigoplus_i a_iRe'_i$: a zero tuple means each $x_i=a_iy_i$ and the vector equals $\sum_i y_if'_i$. Thus it induces an $R$-linear isomorphism $E/N\cong\bigoplus_{i=1}^n R/a_iR$. Step 3 gives length $s_i$ to each cyclic summand. Starting with the zero sum of length zero, apply [lem-weil-pbc-length-additive-short-exact] successively to the split exact sequences $0\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{j-1}R/a_iR\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^j R/a_iR\to R/a_jR\to0$, whose maps are insertion of a zero final coordinate and projection to that coordinate. Induction gives finite length $\ell_R(E/N)=\sum_i s_i$. Length is unchanged by the displayed coordinate isomorphism by Step 3.

source.place: Tag 00IV (lemma-length-additive) applied to the diagonal coordinate quotients of Step 5, and Tag 02MD (definition-ord) for their scalar lengths.

proof.text: We also compute this same sum from an inclusion matrix in arbitrary bases. For any finite free $E$ and $N$ as in Step 5, let $e=(e_i)$ be a chosen $R$-basis of $E$, $f=(f_i)$ one of $N$, and $A$ the matrix defined by $f_j=\sum_i A_{ij}e_i$. Write $e'=eP$ and $f'=fQ$ for the Smith bases, where $P,Q$ and their inverses have entries in $R$. With $D=\operatorname{diag}(a_i)$, the equality $e'D=f'$ gives $PD=AQ$. Specialize [lem-weil-pbc-cauchy-binet] to square matrices ($m=n$): there is just one full-size subset, so $\det(XY)=\det X\det Y$. The Leibniz formula [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant] gives $\det D=\prod_i a_i$ and $\det I=1$ (only the identity permutation contributes); it also shows that evaluating an $R$-matrix over $K$ carries its determinant to the same element in $K$. Apply the product formula to $PP^{-1}=QQ^{-1}=I$ to see that $\det P,\det Q$ are units of $R$. Applying it to $PD=AQ$ now gives $\det A\det Q=\det P\prod_i a_i\ne0$. Taking the exponent valuation calculated in Step 2, and using Step 6, yields $v_R(\det A)=\sum_i s_i=\ell_R(E/N)$. This calculation proves the formula in the chosen bases; it does not assume it is invariant under their change.

source.place: Tag 0F0K (item-cauchy-binet), square case; the agent-written Smith-basis calculation of the DVR case of Tag 02MI (lemma-order-vanishing-determinant).

proof.text: Let $G$ be the matrix of $g$ in the $K$-basis $b$ of Step 1. Use the same basis $f=t^qb$ of $N$ for both inclusions. Its matrix in the basis $b$ of $M$ is $A_M=t^qI$. Its matrix in the basis $g(b)$ of $g(M)$ is a matrix $A_g$ over $R$, since $N\subseteq g(M)$; comparing coordinates in $b$ gives $GA_g=t^qI$. The determinant product and diagonal formulas established in Step 7 imply $\det A_M=t^{qn}$ and $\det G\det A_g=t^{qn}$. By [def-weil-endomorphism-determinant], $\det G=\det_K(g)\ne0$. Hence Steps 2 and 7 give $\ell_R(M/N)=qn$ and $\ell_R(g(M)/N)=qn-v_R(\det_K(g))$, both finite, and therefore $\ell_R(M/N)-\ell_R(g(M)/N)=v_R(\det_K(g))$.

source.place: Tag 02MI (lemma-order-vanishing-determinant), DVR case; the common-lattice matrix relation supplies the full signed formula, including negative determinant valuations.

proof.text: As $N\subseteq H\subseteq M$ and $N\subseteq H\subseteq g(M)$, the maps induced by inclusions and quotient maps give exact sequences $0\to H/N\to M/N\to M/H\to0$ and $0\to H/N\to g(M)/N\to g(M)/H\to0$. For example the kernel of $M/N\to M/H$ consists of precisely the cosets represented by elements of $H$; the second sequence has the same description. By [lem-weil-pbc-length-additive-short-exact] and the finiteness in Step 8, all three modules $H/N,M/H,g(M)/H$ have finite length, and $\ell_R(M/N)=\ell_R(H/N)+\ell_R(M/H)$, $\ell_R(g(M)/N)=\ell_R(H/N)+\ell_R(g(M)/H)$. Subtract these equalities in $\mathbf Z$ and use Step 8. The common term cancels, giving $\ell_R(M/H)-\ell_R(g(M)/H)=v_R(\det_K(g))$, as required.
